The root component's identity verification also failed outright, and 4 of 5 findings checks came back refuted. Since the whole point of this map is to be a deterministic parity baseline, ungrounded claims on its anchor component and an unverified root are exactly the things a P4-7 diff would trip over. The fix is concrete and already scoped: ground the edge from the system-level relationship record and re-verify root against docker-compose.yml, which fits well inside the remaining budget.

tours.title: Language coverage walk
tours.description: Visits every planted language component in importance order to verify the analyzer's tree-sitter path fired for each one. A missing stop here is an analyzer bug, not fixture noise.

steps.title: Python via FastAPI
steps.narration: Start where the Python detection path is exercised: server.py exposes a GET /users/{user_id} handler that gives the analyzer a real FastAPI capability to detect. Every component on this walk exists to exercise a parser, not to do real work.

steps.title: TypeScript and JavaScript
steps.narration: The web client covers two languages at once: client.ts for TypeScript and format.js for JavaScript. It also carries the fixture's only outbound edge, which the next tour examines; here it just needs to appear with both languages attributed.

steps.title: Go with a main entry point
steps.narration: A single main.go provides valid Go syntax plus a main entry point for entry-point detection. Its zero edges are fixture design: it exists to be parsed, not called.

steps.title: Swift and SwiftUI
steps.narration: The fixture's only Swift component. If it is missing from the map, the Swift/SwiftUI detection path went untested — which is why a band-3 component carries the same evidentiary weight as the band-1 api here.

steps.title: Rust and TOML
steps.narration: Cargo.toml plus lib.rs form a minimal but valid crate — 24 lines by design, per the README's 'keep it tiny' constraint. Its isolation exercises Rust parsing, nothing more.

steps.title: Ruby
steps.narration: One 21-line parser.rb covers the Ruby path. Like the Rust crate before it, its under-implementation is intentional; do not read abandonment into a fixture built to parse fast in CI.

steps.title: Markdown and YAML at the root
steps.narration: The walk ends where the config languages live: README.md and docker-compose.yml. This component also carries the fixture's only git activity and its most suspect mechanical signal, which the next tour takes up.

tours.title: The fixture's one relationship
tours.description: Follows the single declared cross-component edge — web client to api over HTTP — which is 100% of the relationship-detection evidence the fixture provides.

steps.title: The declared package
steps.narration: package.json establishes the web client's package identity. It is the declared half of the relationship; the actual call lives one level down.

steps.title: The outbound call
steps.narration: client.ts implements the request that targets services/api over HTTP. This is the only outbound edge in the entire fixture, so the mechanical 'zone of uselessness' finding here — nothing consumes the web client — is fixture design, not a defect.

steps.title: The receiving endpoint
steps.narration: The edge terminates at the FastAPI handler in server.py, bound to port 8000. The boundary-strength signal says this one seam is separated by a real contract, which is exactly what the fixture was planted to make detectable.

tours.title: Where mechanical signals need a second look
tours.description: Two places where the analyzer's mechanical signals could mislead a parity diff: a port claim attributed to a markdown root, and edge counts that stop short of naming the caller.

steps.title: The port that isn't here
steps.narration: The analyzer records 'listens on a port' on a component whose only files are README.md and docker-compose.yml. The port is an attribution from the compose file's declared db/cache services, not a root-level bind — freeze it unexplained and the parity snapshot preserves an artifact.

steps.title: What the edge count actually proves
steps.narration: Adjudication found the api's own evidence shows one inbound edge and one capability, but does not by itself name services/web/src as the caller or prove the api is unique in either respect. The relationship is real; the superlatives around it were not evidenced. This is what deterministic grounding looks like in practice.

lenses.name: Component-local evidence cannot support fixture-global claims
lenses.observation: All four adjudication rejections on services/api share one shape: a claim scoped to the whole fixture ('only capability', 'highest inbound count', 'the caller is services/web/src') backed by evidence scoped to one component. The enrichment per-component context structurally cannot ground the cross-component claims the parity anchor most needs.
lenses.why_it_matters: An analyzer developer diffing P4-7 against this baseline needs the web→api edge stated with its endpoints, but every attempt to state it at the component level was correctly struck down. The system-level relationship record, not component enrichment, is the only place that claim can be grounded — and the map should draw it from there.

lenses.name: Importance banding inverts the fixture's own value ordering
lenses.observation: The mechanical bands rank services/api first by fan-in and push the Swift, Rust, and Ruby components to bands 3–5, but in a coverage fixture each language component is worth exactly one parser path — a dropped libs/rubylib is the same severity of analyzer bug as a dropped services/api. The census (3 grounded at opus, 6 at sonnet) suggests effort followed the bands rather than the coverage goal.
lenses.why_it_matters: A parity diff reader scans for missing languages, not for load-bearing components; a map that spends its confidence on the head and leaves tail components thinly grounded protects exactly the wrong thing.
